explain: TypeScript **infers** `T = string` from the argument, so the return type `T | undefined` becomes `string | undefined`. `T` only exists inside the signature; at the call site it's replaced by the real type. `any` is what you'd get from the non-generic `any[]` version.

q: A colleague wants `describe<T>(value: T)` to return `"text"` when `T` is `string`. Why can't they write `if (T === string)`?
options: Types are erased before the code runs, so `T` doesn't exist at runtime. Check the value instead: `typeof value === "string"`
It works, but only with `T extends string`
explain: TypeScript removes every type when it compiles to JavaScript. There's no `T` left to compare. Generics describe the relationship between inputs and outputs **at the call site**. At runtime you only have values, so you check the value with `typeof` (which is narrowing, from the Core section).

q: `function pushItem<T>(list: readonly T[], item: T): T[]`. Which calls compile? Select all that apply.
explain: Using one `T` for both parameters says the item has the same type as the list's elements. `pushItem([1, 2], "x")` infers `T = number` from the array and then rejects `"x"`. If you really want a mixed list, you can pass the type argument yourself, `<string | number>`, and both arguments fit. Use separate parameters `<A, B>` when the types are meant to differ.

q: Why does this generic not compile?
options: A bare `T` could be any type, like `number` or `null`, so TypeScript won't assume it has `.name`
`T` must be written `<T>` on every parameter
explain: Nothing stops a caller from writing `names([1, 2, 3])`, so the compiler is right to refuse `item.name`. To allow it, you need to tell TypeScript that `T` has *at least* a `name`. That's a **generic constraint**, `<T extends { name: string }>`, and it's the next node.
